challenges.name: cohesion-coupling-quiz
challenges.title: What the numbers say about helpers.ts and the coupon rule
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the CodeDev backend: the commits behind the last coupon changes, and the import counts of utils/helpers.ts. Decide whether each statement is True or False.

questions.question:
git log --name-only for the last three changes to the coupon rule:

feat: coupons can have a minimum price
  src/orders/application/apply-coupon.ts
  src/catalog/domain/pricing.ts
  src/notifications/templates/receipt.ts

fix: 100% coupons charged 1 VND
  src/orders/application/apply-coupon.ts
  src/catalog/domain/pricing.ts
  src/notifications/templates/receipt.ts

feat: coupons expire at midnight
  src/orders/application/apply-coupon.ts
  src/catalog/domain/pricing.ts
  src/notifications/templates/receipt.ts

Statement: "The coupon rule has low cohesion: code that changes together, for one reason, is spread over three modules."
questions.explanation: True. Cohesion asks whether things that change together live together. Every coupon change, for one business reason, had to edit orders, catalog and notifications, so the rule is scattered: low cohesion, and three modules coupled through one rule. The usual misconception is to judge cohesion by file names or folder tidiness; the evidence that counts is what changes together in the history.

questions.question:
The import count for src/utils/helpers.ts:

$ grep -rl "utils/helpers" src | wc -l
23

helpers.ts itself imports nothing from the rest of src. So fan-in = 23, fan-out = 0, and instability I = 0 / (23 + 0) = 0.00.

Statement: "I = 0.00 means helpers.ts is safe to change: an edit there cannot break any other module."
questions.explanation: False. Instability I = fan-out / (fan-in + fan-out). I = 0 means the module depends on nothing and 23 files depend on it: it is stable in the sense of hard to change, because every edit can break any of those 23 importers. The misconception is reading "stable" as "safe to edit". A module like this should change rarely and contain only code that truly belongs together; a grab-bag of helpers is the opposite.

challenges.name: coupling-report
challenges.title: Measure coupling: fan-in, fan-out and instability per module
challenges.description:
Before the CodeDev team splits anything, it wants numbers. Write couplingReport(input) in main.ts. It returns the report as an array of lines; the test runner prints one line each.

Input (JSON on stdin): { "modules": string[], "dependencies": [from, to][], "threshold": number }. Module names are unique. A dependency ["orders", "catalog"] means the orders module imports something from catalog.

Rules:
- A dependency listed more than once counts once.
- A self-dependency (from and to are the same module) is ignored.
- fanIn(X) = how many different modules depend on X. fanOut(X) = how many different modules X depends on.
- Instability I = fanOut / (fanIn + fanOut), rounded with Math.round(I * 100) / 100 and printed with toFixed(2). A module with no dependencies in either direction has I = 0.00.
- One line per module, in the order of input.modules: "<name> in=<fanIn> out=<fanOut> I=<I>", followed by " HIGH" when fanIn + fanOut is greater than threshold. Example: orders in=1 out=3 I=0.75 HIGH
- If a dependency names a module that is not in modules, the report is exactly one line, "error: unknown module <name>", for the first unknown name: dependencies in input order, from checked before to.
hints: If orders imports catalog in three different files, the list may contain ["orders", "catalog"] three times. How many modules does orders depend on? What data structure makes a repeated pair count once?

Do the work in three passes: first check every name against the module list (stop at the first unknown one), then build the set of distinct pairs while skipping from === to, then for each module count the pairs where it is the target (fanIn) and where it is the source (fanOut). Watch the module with no pairs at all: 0 / 0 is NaN, not 0.

The same counting on a different graph: a team chat app has users -> rooms, rooms -> messages, users -> messages, messages -> messages and users -> rooms again. Distinct pairs without the self-pair: users -> rooms, rooms -> messages, users -> messages. So rooms has in=1 out=1, I = 1 / 2 = 0.50; messages has in=2 out=0, I = 0.00; users has in=0 out=2, I = 1.00. With threshold 1, all three modules have a total of 2, so all three are flagged HIGH.
